Privacy search engine company DuckDuckGo has released a new survey revealing the amount of personal information users share with AI chatbots, as well as how little many people understand about where these conversations end up. Details are as follows.

Survey shows AI users share more information than they realise

In a survey published today, DuckDuckGo highlighted several privacy concerns related to the way AI chatbots are used, including the fact that nearly one-third of users have told an AI something they would not say to a friend, family member, colleague, or healthcare professional. Among those who identify as AI enthusiasts, this figure rises to 56%.

DuckDuckGo had this to say:

The company pointed out that, among nearly 2,000 American adults who participated in the survey, 53% did not know or were unsure that most chatbots use conversations by default to train their models, while only 25% knew that law enforcement agencies could obtain AI conversation records through a subpoena.

The survey results also revealed a significant behavioural difference between parents and non-parents, with parents or guardians who have children at home confiding in AI at almost twice the rate of non-parents. DuckDuckGo stated that "among parents who use AI, 43% have told an AI something they have never shared with anyone," while "among AI users without children at home, this figure drops to 25%."

DuckDuckGo believes that AI companies, through advertising campaigns and media exposure, encourage users to view chatbots as confidants, but these conversations may not be as private as users are led to believe.

On the topic of trust, the survey found that people's confidence in large AI companies to protect their data is only slightly higher than their confidence in the US government. However, scepticism towards both remains high: 39% of respondents said they have no trust at all in large AI companies, while the figure for the government is even higher at 48%.

Finally, DuckDuckGo believes users still have an opportunity to change the way they handle AI privacy, particularly because people's habits with chatbots are still relatively new:

"When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, many people feel it's 'too late, my data is already out there,' but the most valuable piece of information you can share with Big Tech is actually your next question, not what you asked days, months, or even years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more privacy-focused online services."

The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data handling policies.
